body:
My experience is not something that I am proud of.
When I was 16 I tried Percocet for the first time.  I only took one and it was no big deal to me.  My mom has back problems so she had a constant supply of them.  Their presence in the house was never a big deal, until one day when I was 17 and having a bad day I went into my mom's purse and popped three 10mg pills to make myself forget about whatever had been bothering me.  I often look back at that day and think about how different my life would be if I had never found out what opiates could really do.  In the weeks that fallowed I popped them constantly, whenever something was wrong, to dull it away, or sometimes just to 'take the edge off' when I was nervous.  I secretly became addicted but hid it under a fake stomach problem.  I would make myself cry, pretending to be in pain, just so my mom would give me some.
This went on for about a year, and then someone told me about fentanyl.  I had no idea that the patches my mom wore were actually filled with a drug at least 10 times better then Percocet.  My first time getting high on fentanyl was amazing.  I stayed up the whole night, having sex with my boyfriend, cleaning my house, in this intense state of euphoria.
I began taking the patches more and more often.  My memory was vastly affected by the fentanyl, and I would often find things in my closet that I had no memory whatsoever of buying.  When I went to the movies with my friends I would just stare at the screen, and after we left I'd have no idea what the movie had been about.  I found myself in a horrible addiction to a drug that is more potent that heroin.  It was prescription though, so I felt safe.
That is until I woke up in ICU with on a respirator.  The doctor told me I was as close to death as you get, short of dying.  'Oops,' I told myself, and made a mental note not to take two patches at a time.  I lied to everyone and told them it was sleeping pills that had made me breath in my own puke.  They released me with a couple oxygen tanks.
I returned 3 months later.  The same doctor worked to save my life.  He looked at me and shook his head.  I let them all think I tried to kill myself, when really I was just trying to get high.
My wake up call snuck up on me.  I began to lose friends who could tell something was wrong, my mom found empty patches in my room, and I was expelled from school for being high.  My life was over.  There is no high that is worth the embarrassment that I felt when my secret came out.  Luckily, I had my mom.  She held my hand though the horrible withdrawals and pleaded with me, crying, to get help.  I didn't want to die.  Worse, I didn't want my mom to lose her only daughter.  I entered a 90-day rehab center and never looked back.  I will always be a recovering addict.  Recently I had oral surgery and could only use tylenol.  It hurt, but its the price I'm willing to pay.
